records.title: Show HN: Open-source, real-time object tracking for live video feeds
records.author: aryaman_darda
records.storyText:
I type "forklift" on a live warehouse camera, and tamserve finds and tracks both forklifts, including the one driving in. Then I add "person" without stopping it.

tamserve runs Meta's SAM 3 on live camera feeds. SAM 3's own tracker handles one recorded video at a time, runs at about 8 fps, and runs out of memory on long videos. tamserve uses SAM 3 to find objects every few frames and a lightweight tracker (EdgeTAM) to follow them in between, with one copy of each model shared across all your cameras.

*On one RTX 4090:*

* *Any object you name:* 4x faster than SAM 3's tracker, at 92% of its accuracy * *People:* 16 cameras at once, 14x less GPU per frame, and slightly more accurate than SAM 3 (89.6 vs 87.8 HOTA) * *Memory:* flat at 3.5 GB on a 3,000 frame video, where SAM 3 runs out at frame 423

*Worth a look if you're building:*

* Warehouse or factory safety (forklifts, pallets, hard hats) * Security or retail camera analytics * Home or elder care monitoring * Robotics, wildlife or lab monitoring * Annotation tools for long videos

`pip install "tamserve[sam3]"`

Please give me any and all feedback or edit tamserve to meet your needs, and a star helps if you find it useful!

We think there's a better solution - cloud computers engineered for agents.

Simular started three years ago to build out the full stack of an autonomous computer. box is our attempt to give agents a body to live in.

Our computer use outperformed Opus and GPT on OSWorld, costing fewer tokens. https://thenewstack.io/sai-agent-osworld-benchmark/

Copy/paste one command into your agent to start:

"Set up box from https://box.simular.ai/install"

records.title: Show HN: My OSS Claude Meetings alternative that works with any agent or call
records.author: wanderingstan
records.storyText:
Since February, I've been developing an agent-in-calls solution with a friend. With the announcement of Claude Meetings last week, it's now time to announce Vibeconferencing: an open-source project with even more functionality, support for any agent (Codex, Muse, local ollama, etc), and support for more calling platforms: Google Meet, Zoom, MS Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram, and phone calls (via Twilio).

Architecture diagram: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wanderingstan/vibeconf-app...

The premise is simple: give your normal agent session the tools it needs to operate all major calling platforms, and teach it basic etiquette of how to behave in a call with others. A simple `/join-call` and boom! your session is talking to you in the call. Anything your agent can do in chat, it can do on the call. The agent is bridged to the calling platforms via a cross-platform electron app. (The raw guts of interacting with calling platforms is abstracted as the npm library `@vibeconferencing/calls`, if you'd rather roll your own.)

Everything runs locally and uses your own local agent. (Tho the optional shared whiteboard feature does require being logged in on our server.) It runs on MacOS, Windows, and Linux. (Windows version is not well tested.)

Speech generation is done either by Elevenlabs or the OSS Voicebox, with a fallback to the OS's default app (e.g. `say` on MacOS). Voicebox: https://github.com/jamiepine/voicebox

Speech recognition is done either by the calling platforms' own captioning services (Meet, Zoom, Teams), or with Whistle for those without captioning (WhatsApp, Telegram, Twilio). Whistle: https://cactuscompute.com/blog/whistle

The etiquette was the most fun to code, although done with the knowledge that it's a temporary fix until true interactive voice models are merged with the power of frontier text chat models. We have experimental support for the OpenAI realtime API, but it seems to have been trained as a customer support agent, so it's hard to keep it from dominating multi-person conversations!

Highlights from the last nine months of dogfooding and early users:

- A WhatsApp bot for my father, an elderly WW2 veteran, that has access to the 20,000 photos he scanned. He can call it to see and hear about any aspect of his life. https://youtu.be/Rs-Z1YeLt98

- Collaboratively built a website for a friend's non-profit, with her amazed that she could ask for site changes and see the site change in realtime. https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iSRgY8JGJ0liOzHMl2bOGNd9jwq...

- My friend Matt is currently road-tripping across the US, talking with his Codex sessions to develop his Golf app. https://youtu.be/a3uNUdIwqVY

- Our friend Bethany uses her bot "Taylor Script", in calls and classrooms with coding students to act as the super-smart TA who can answer technical questions, and monitors student progress. https://youtu.be/c8mZKkcxhJo

- I begin most days with a check-in call with my bot Jimmy, where we discuss open repo issues while I have breakfast. https://youtu.be/2uQIR83LwY0 (Apologies for eating with my mouth open...)

- In a standup, Seth's bot created a video ad for the service itself, within a call. https://x.com/vibeconf/status/2104427917816234257?s=20

Security: There is nothing built in, so only use this on calls with people that you trust. However, I've been amazed at how injection-resistant it has appeared to be on it's own; e.g. my agent asking consent from me before doing things asked by others on the call.

Overall, this was a "time machine" experiment (to borrow my old Reality Labs' Research terminology) to experience agents-in-calls before it was purpose built. Claude Meetings just showed that we were thinking in the right direction, and I'm excited to see where this goes!

This is a small experimental project built by two friends, so it is rough around the edges, and we'd love feedback and pull requests.

records.title: Show HN: A booking page that handles payment and sends a Zoom/Meet/Discord link
records.author: poteresting
records.storyText:
Programming used to be the fun part. Sit with a problem for a week, get it working at night, the thing is yours. The idea of bootstrapping your SaaS and breaking out in the industry used to be exciting, but now everything is a prompt and can be built by anyone, in a weekend.

What nobody wants to do is keep it running and maintain it. I think big SaaS will survive, but a small SaaS business is hard to sell. I know building is cheap, maintaining is the actual work, and the part I decided to take on.

Since the end of July I have been building this alone. Consultants, Coaches, tutors, I know are selling sessions with linktree + calendly + stripe link or "dm me on discord", and also struggle using discord as the place to host the session, like Google Meet or Zoom. Which means making a voice channel by hand for every call. Now it's one page: people pick a time, pay if it's a paid session, and the call link is made for them on discord, zoom or google, sent in the email.

I built a discord bot that turns discord into a meeting platform like Zoom or Google Meet. Add the bot to your server, run /setup, members can book with /book on the server or from the page, and 15 min before the start it makes a voice channel where only the creator and the booker can see.

One thing I'm not sure about: no fixed price. A booking is a request with an offer starting from the base price, the creator accepts or declines. Clever or annoying, you tell me.

Take a look at mine https://shinetr.ee/poty or type /book in https://discord.gg/SfEVf2yFPT. The dashboard lets you fully customize how you would like.

I don't know if this takes off. Trying to get users right now and their feedback. But the few months of building it were the first time in a while that I closed the laptop and felt like I made something, and I wanted to put it in front of people who would get that especially with all the fear mongering of software development is over.

If you sell sessions, or you want to build something like this together, write me. I will be in the comments all day.

records.title: Show HN: Belay – formal verification for SQLite migrations and queries in Lean 4
records.author: neprotivo
records.storyText:
Hi, I'm Tzanko and I'm the author of Belay.

Belay is a Lean 4 library for doing formal verification of SQLite queries and migrations. It implements a semantic model of a subset of SQLite, validated by differential tests that compare the output against native SQLite.

With Belay I wanted to see how difficult it is to use formal verification for everyday development tasks. It turns out it can be made not much harder than writing an integration test: you state the claim, the agent writes the proof, and Lean's kernel checks it, so the only thing you have to read is the claim (longer write-up on the motivation and agent workflow: https://vihren.dev/blog/20261112-belay/).

While a migration is being written, your agent can run #sql_check, which searches small databases for counterexamples to a claim, and is as easy to run as a linter.

Once the migration is settled, the agent writes a proof of the claims you need, for example that the migration preserves the results of existing queries and succeeds on valid data.

Currently Belay supports a subset of SQLite 3.51.0, cross-checked against native SQLite on 5,768 differential test cases, most of which come from SQLite's own test suite. Unsupported SQL is rejected with a reason and never approximated. Not every rule of the model has had a human audit yet. The model covers single-connection operational semantics only: it says nothing about query plans, locks, concurrency or crash behavior.

I think this approach can make formal verification as routine as testing, though two things stand in the way. The first is coverage: the model has to cover the full semantics of SQLite and all of its recent versions, and the same work has to be done for other engines such as PostgreSQL and ClickHouse. The second is proof cost: the proofs of common claims are still long for the agent to write, and they have to become short. I'm looking for design partners who want this for their workloads on SQLite or other open-source databases, because a real workload is the best guide to what to cover first. The models that come out of that work become part of Belay as open source. Reach out at contact@vihren.dev.

If you know a tricky SQLite edge case where the model might diverge from native SQLite, or a gnarly migration bug you've hit in production, I'd love to test it and hear your thoughts.

records.title: Show HN: Turn any selfie into a 3D head you can stretch like Mario 64
records.author: DJSnackySnack
records.storyText:
Floppy Face is an app I built that transforms any selfie photo into a 3D head you can pull and stretch like the opening of Mario 64.

The app runs on Three.js and WebGL, so it performs smoothly on a browser or phone. When a photo is uploaded, Floppy Face uses MediaPipe to detect facial landmarks and map them onto a 468-point face template with estimated depth. The mesh is then subdivided for smoother stretching.

The app procedurally constructs the back of the head and uses sampled skin and hair colors to help blend it smoothly. The app then adds 3d-modeled ears and a Mario-inspired cap to complete the effect.

When a user pulls on the photo, a custom soft brush moves nearby vertices to deform the face in a smooth, predictable way. When you release, a custom spring effect creates a satisfying rubbery bounce.

records.title: Show HN: Temper: Declare your system and fails the build when no proof
records.author: dm03514
records.storyText:
Hello Everyone! Like many of you, I've been using LLM heavily for software development.

Models have been getting better and better, requiring me to open my IDE less and less.

I've found myself thinking in terms of specifying the system boundaries, invariants and lattices of values and types that the system needs to handle.

I created Temper to codify this framework. Temper is a structured way to specify functional requirements, invariants, and lattices and link them up to test evidence.

This provides a rich coverage view and helps me to think about functionality in a structured way. Over the last 2 days i've been using temper to uncover bugs in a number of foundational data libraries, that power many of the most popular data tools in the industry:

https://turbolytics.github.io/temper/findings/

I'd love to hear your feedback! Are you using any sort of spec driven development? Happy to answer any questions or to sit down and walk through integrating Temper into your project and CI!

records.title: Show HN: T'Pico, a classless CSS library for modern browsers
records.author: dday9
records.storyText:
Lucas Larroche declared on Oct 4, 2026 that he was archiving PicoCSS and it really upset me. Here was a library that I promoted, used in several websites, and really saw as the future of minimalistic web development.

Starting last month sometime, I decided that I would rewrite the library to not only address some of the issues Lucas outlined such as using OKLCH colors, cascade layers, and the Popover API, but to also make some architectural decisions that I didn't agree. Last week, I finally pushed everything up on GitHub. There is a full demo on jsfiddle too: https://jsfiddle.net/bLpsf2jd/

The name I decided to go with is T'Pico, which is a double entendre not only representing the minimalistic nature of Pico's original vision but also as a play on the Cajun norm of putting "T" in front of people's names (like father "Bob" and son "T'Bob"); in a sense T'Pico is a child born out of PicoCSS.

T'Pico wasn't a one-to-one rewrite of PicoCSS, it is a complete rewrite, not a drop-in replacement. Outside of adding a few new components such as the offcanvas, classless version of the dropdown component, the toolbar component, etc., there were some things I left out entirely. For example, rather than hijacking the RTL attribute to manage visual appearances of components, I felt like it was better left out entirely and allow the native RTL browser rendering do its thing.

I am looking for feedback on improving the library. I have been going through the original Pico discussions to look for what people were talking about there and even implemented a bit of it when doing the initial rewrite.

Full disclaimer if you decide to check out the repository: I basically gave ChatGPT my source code for T'Pico and told it to write the documentation for me. This saved me hours in building out the documentation. I know some will poo-poo on that, but it really helped me with the tedious stuff that I'm not really good at. In case you can't tell by this post, I cant spel are grammur goodly.

Anyways, I look forward to hearing y'all's feedback and let's keep the move to more minimalistic web development going!

Hi HN, since some time I have been experimenting with a new way to work with AI agents, instead of chatting with them in the usual sense, I wanted to work with them collaboratively (like people usually do in google docs or confluence).

I think the chat based interface we use for these coding agents doesn't extend well to other use cases, like researching, thinking... or just having a general introspective session with AI.

I thought of having a simple markdown editor (like Notion), where you can just dump your thoughts (or documents) and then the AI agents can work off of them. I wanted to the app to be completely local so I don't depend on any cloud providers and can eventually run entirely offline with self-hosted LLMs in the future.

This is a completely new way to use and interact with AI agents, where your document is the main control surface. The AI agents can give back nicely formatted tables, images and other content. You can use this for planning, brainstorming, researching and more.

You can also create custom buttons which can trigger the same task again (like summarising new tickets assigned to you), these tasks can be run on some interval as well. Everything happens in the background daemon running on your machine, so you can just close the tabs/browser, and the Pi agents continue to run.

It is fairly extensible as well. Do give it a shot !

records.title: Show HN: Heardloom – Preserve immigrant family stories before they're lost
records.author: westdragon
records.storyText:
I built Heardloom (https://heardloom.com) to help immigrant families capture their life stories before they're lost.

My parents immigrated from China, and I believe all immigrants have extraordinary stories. Leaving behind everyone you know to start over in an unfamiliar country makes you a risk-taker almost by definition.

Yet, I know very little of my family stories. To be honest, my Chinese was never good enough to truly understand the fine details of their stories. I know that my grandma's mom died when she was a child, but I don't know her emotions or how it affected her relationship with her dad. I don't know how she became a factory engineer - what inspired her and how she developed her interests.

I'll never know either. My grandma passed away unexpectedly. She practically raised my sister and me while my parents worked 80+hr weeks to provide for us. I spent over a decade with her, and I'll spend the rest of my life regretting that I never truly got to know her.

I just had my own kids, and I want to make sure they know where they come from and their family's extraordinary stories. I wanted something like Storyworth or Remento, but they were only in English and too hard for my parents to use.

That's why I made Heardloom. My family can have casual conversations in Chinese to Lana (named after my grandma). All of the stories get translated to English and turned into a family book. I also get to share my stories and photos to my family, so they get to see my life now in America.

I would love any feedback, and I'm happy to help anyone get set up. This would make the perfect gift over the holidays for any parents or grandparents.

records.title: Show HN: AI Spar – Turn conflicting AI answers into a structured debate
records.author: wwind123
records.storyText:
Over the last couple of years, I have observed many people (including myself) researching tricky topics by asking the same question to multiple AI's. If those answers conflict, we manually copy the answers back-and-forth between the AI apps to make them debate each other, to get a fuller picture of the topic.

I developed AI Spar to organize and automate this debate process. When the user asks a question:

1) Multiple AI's answer the question independent of each other.

2) An analyzer (also an AI model) finds the consensuses and disagreements between those answers, and what important points are missed by which answer.

3) For each disagreement point, each AI tries to defend its stance when presented with its original answer and the other side's opinion (it can concede if it feels the other side is right); and for each missed point, each AI tries to clarify whether it agrees with the point.

4) If all disagreement points have consensus, or the debate has reached max number of rounds, then go to 5); otherwise, go to 3) for the next round of debate with the latest arguments from each side.

5) The analyzer summarizes the debate, synthesizes a final answer, and lists the consensus points, resolved disagreements, unresolved disagreements, and clarified missed points.

Note that it might feel slow compared to those AI apps, because of all the steps taken above. Also worth a disclaimer: even if all AI's eventually agree on one point, that doesn't necessarily mean it's correct.

Some friends have been testing this system. They mention that sometimes reading the back-and-forth debate details is a lot more fun than reading the final synthesis.

Without signing in, you can try two separate questions, with entry-level models from 3 AI providers (Gemini, GPT, Claude).

Signing in enables additional features: asking follow-up questions, attaching images or PDFs, saving and sharing conversations. Also, stronger models from these providers are available for signed-in users. In addition, you can enable web-search grounded debates, and optional fact-checking during the debates. You pay as you go, no subscription at this point. Cost of each debate depends on the models and settings. We also support BYOK for these providers, with a separate system fee. CLI/API access is also available if you need them.

An interesting debate example: https://aispar.app/share/5f503127-4b4a-4c5c-9b2a-74081016b68... "Should junior developers use coding agents from their first day? " Even though all three AI's (Gemini, GPT, Claude) initially broadly agree on the surface, after the debate, each has made pretty big changes on the substance, and at the end there's still unresolved disagreement.

records.title: Show HN: An API for word timestamps from speech, 75% within 20ms
records.author: jasperstory
records.storyText:
Hey HN, we're Yarn (W24) and we make a video editing app for startups, and we built Quebec (https://quebec.yarn.so), an API that gives you accurate word timestamps from speech. We needed it because cutting a word even 50ms off from its true timing can ruin talking head footage (examples in the write up).

Accurate word timestamps usually come from a forced aligner, which takes the speech audio and a transcript and works out exactly when each word starts and ends. We weren't satisfied with the accuracy of Montreal Forced Aligner (MFA) or new models like ElevenLabs Cue (https://elevenlabs.io/blog/cue-aligner). Giving LLMs access to a waveform/spectrogram didn't help much either.

So we built our own. There are two particularly interesting parts: - We wrote our own decoder around MFA's acoustic model that only lets each word land within 200ms of the rough timings. That made search small enough to solve exactly, so we don't need to use MFA's beam search. - We added a small CNN, built on the first two layers of Whisper Tiny, that nudges each word boundary by up to 50ms. We couldn't find enough hand-labelled speech that allowed for commercial use, so we had Gemini label our own (17k word boundaries). It took a couple of hours and cost under $200. A net trained on Gemini's labels scored the same as one trained on human labels (73.9% vs. 74%).

One way to measure accuracy is % of word boundaries within 20ms of hand labels. Here are the results on Buckeye (hand-labelled American speech that we didn't train on):

- Quebec 75%

- MFA 61%

- ElevenLabs Cue 30%

If you want to try it, it's free until tomorrow night. You can point your agent at our docs at https://quebec.yarn.so, and send audio on its own or with your own transcript. After that, it costs $0.32 per hour with no signup (minimum $10 top-up). We serve it at cost. Caveats: only tested in English and slower than ElevenLabs.

Let us know if Quebec works well for you, and send us any samples that work badly (you can email support at yarn dot so). Also let us know if you've built or found a better aligner. In theory we would just switch to a better aligner, although we would probably just push a bit harder to make ours better.

Thanks!

Jasper

records.title: Show HN: Darkroomfinder.org – A Directory of Photography Darkrooms
records.author: stokesj84
records.storyText:
I built darkroomfinder.org, a directory of photography darkrooms, as a React single page app (SPA), because I wanted to understand how SPAs work and I wanted to scale to hundreds or thousands of cities without managing routes and pages for each of them. The site currently lists over 350 darkrooms across over 50 countries.

However in deciding to build a SPA I failed to realize the downsides of SPAs for SEO. As an SPA darkroomfinder.org only has one route, i.e. darkroomfinder.org. Therefore GoogleBot only indexes the root domain and if someone searches for "Darkrooms" the site might surface in Google Search, but if a user searches "San Francisco Darkrooms" Google Search is much less likely to return darkroomfinder.org as nothing indicates the site has information about San Francisco.

Solving this SEO problem while maintaining the simplicity of the SPA turned out to be a challenge but I think I have arrived at a solution that checks most of the desired boxes at the cost of being tied more closely to Cloudflare's infrastructure. Cloudflare, the DNS and CDN for darkroomfinder.org, has a serverless primitive, Cloudflare Workers. These Cloudflare Workers are distributed at the edge, have KV caches, and can intercept specific paths. So my solution to having both an SPA and indexable city routes is to have Cloudflare Workers cache the city data and intercept city routes directed at darkroomfinder.org returning an HTML page with the city data and the full React SPA which boots over the HTML page. So technically it's one SPA served to many routes. GoogleBot in traversing one of these city routes, like darkroomfinder.org/san-francisco, will index the HTML page while humans using browsers receive the same HTML which the React SPA boots over.

Part of the project that remains unsolved is data collection and validation. Darkroom discovery is automated by agents running daily scans for unlisted darkrooms. But a human still has to validate that the discovered darkrooms exist and try to determine what capabilities they have such as B&W or color developing etc. I am currently working on an automated reachability and vitality checker to determine if the darkrooms already in the directory are still active, since photography darkrooms sometimes cease operations long before taking down their websites or social feeds.

darkroomfinder.org

records.title: Show HN: Revix AI – PR review against the standards your repo follows
records.author: oscarestudillom
records.storyText:
Hello, I’m Oscar. I’ve been leading dev teams from Barcelona with my cofounder Uri for a long time. We pushed the use of AI a lot, allowing an increase in the code shipment velocity, but our job as seniors moved from building to just reviewing. We also started to see a lot of drift in how devs were doing the code, less standards, less control, which caused more bugs and differences between what product department asked and what we shipped. It was impossible for us to keep reviewing everything by hand, so we decided to clone how we review as humans into a product: Revix AI.

In easy words, Revix main strength is that it extracts from your repo all the good practices and team standards, then on every pull request comments if anything moves from that. That, paired with PR status badges and targeted notifications allowed us to reduce review time by 54% on many teams, while increasing the confidence and reducing bugs on production.

We know there are other similar products around and they work fine, but we found that they trust too much on the LLM and focus just on bug hunting. Our philosophy goes further, we created a system that reviews the same as a senior engineer would do, not catching just bugs. We achieved to comment only on things devs actually fix and stop the noise.

Revix AI works on GitHub, Gitlab, Bitbucket and can sync with many other tools like Slack, Jira, Linear etc. Please feel free to request any other tool that we still do not support. We offer free reviews for any open source project, and for companies we do price per seat including a 14 days free trial.

If you want to see Revix AI working, you can check this example PR: https://github.com/revix-app/fastapi-revix/pull/1 And here is one from an open source project that use many other reviewers so you can compare: https://github.com/ontogr/ontogr-agent-memory/pull/19

We want to work very closely with the community, so feel free to try it out and give us feedback, we love to keep improving and listen to all the customers and developers that try our tool.

records.title: Show HN: LingDongNews, a small desktop news ticker for your own feeds
records.author: funiqlab
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I made LingDongNews, a small desktop news ticker.

With agents doing more of the work, we’re left with lots of little gaps in the day. They’re too short and scattered to do much else, so I made a small tool to check the news whenever there’s a moment.

English demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kb6YXzWzQ-0

It stays on top as a single scrolling line. Click a story to expand it, then collapse it when you’re done.

You choose the sources: It supports RSS, Atom, JSON Feed, JSON endpoints and custom adapters.

You can highlight keywords you care about, or optionally connect your own AI API to highlight news matching your interests. Other news remain visible.

The interface is available in English and Chinese. The bundled sources are mainly Chinese financial news, but you can disable them and use your own feeds.

records.title: Show HN: Call Nara. An AI voice companion built with older people in mind
records.author: anthonyjg_sec
records.storyText:
Call Nara: someone to talk to, any time

Call Nara is a simple voice companion for older people, and for anyone who spends long days alone. You tap once and talk. There's no typing.

Nara greets you by name, asks how you are, chats and listens. Just ask by voice, and she can play music, hymns and movies, read from the Bible, and look through photos that you or your family have added, reading out the captions and chatting about them. If you nominate a family member, friend or carer, she can let them know if you seem upset or distressed.

Call Nara was designed with older people in mind, and with the families and friends who love them. It's built for everyone, so no one is left behind. Whatever your age, Nara is here for you.

Available now on iPhone and iPad (iOS only for now). Feel free to check it out

records.title: Show HN: Sip pacer to help you drink slower
records.author: OzBuilds
records.storyText:
It's a new feature I've added to Pour Decision.

The idea is:

1. Set an interval on your phone and slip it in your pocket

2. The phone vibrates in your pocket on every interval

3. Condition yourself to have sips when you feel the vibration

Benefits:

- You end up drinking way less in a night than you normally would

- You don't feel like you're moderating cus you're never without a drink

- It's discreet so people you're drinking with won't know you're doing this

This is sort of like a HIIT-timer, but to preserve battery I took another approach. It works by pre-scheduling on-device notifications when you start the timer. iOS allows apps to schedule up to 64 notifications. If you were to set say 5-minute intervals, that covers the next 320 minutes - more than 5 hours. The phone uses no battery in between intervals, and only wakes up the device once every 5 minutes, so battery drain is negligible.

Here's a write-up about it if interested:

https://pourdecision.app/blog/sip-pacing-method

records.title: Show HN: Open Academy – Math Academy-style courses for any subject
records.author: Jonathanvw
records.storyText:
Open Academy is an open-source app inspired by Math Academy (https://mathacademy.com/). You use it to create courses on any subject, taught in a similar way.

If you're unfamiliar with Math Academy, it's a maths learning site with short lessons, lots of practice questions, and reviews that bring old topics back before you forget them. I really enjoyed using it to study maths, but I couldn't find anything similar for other subjects. At the same time, I was using AI a lot to learn new topics but my lessons had no structure. So I built Open Academy to bridge that gap.

You create courses with your AI of choice through the CLI, ideally grounded in your own notes or content from the web. The app handles the rest, which includes prerequisite locks, quizzes and spaced review (FSRS).

I don't intend to make a managed version of this. The repo and the demo include example courses: Maths for ML, ML Foundations, Deep Learning, Transformers and LLMs, LLM Inference and Reinforcement Learning so you can get a feel fo rit.

MIT licensed. Runs with Docker, on Vercel with Neon, or fork it do with it as you please as far as hosting is concerned.

Demo: https://open-academy-demo.vercel.app

The problem I kept seeing was most founders know they should post regularly, but they don’t. Scheduling tools aren’t the hard part. The hard part is deciding what to say, following daily trends in your niche and actually creating and posting consistently as Social media algorithms rewards not just quality but volume as well

It has helped few businesses grow their social accounts from zero to few thousand followers without any paid promotions.
